title: What Actually Happens When You Copy and Paste?
sources: Wikipedia, 'Cut, copy, and paste': the clipboard is temporary storage; on most systems only one clipboard location exists, so another cut or copy overwrites the previously stored information; the term comes from manuscript editing where people cut paragraphs from a page with scissors and pasted them onto another page; Larry Tesler proposed the names cut, copy and paste, and from 1974 he and colleagues at Xerox PARC implemented text editors using them; Apple Lisa (1983) / Macintosh (1984) popularized Cmd X/C/V

Alex Harri, 'The web's clipboard, and how it stores data of different types': the clipboard stores information in multiple representations (MIME types such as text/plain, text/html, image/png); a plain editor like VS Code reads only text/plain while Google Docs reads text/html and keeps formatting
NPR Weekend Edition (Feb 2020), remembrance of Larry Tesler: Tesler and Tim Mott at Xerox in the 1970s helped create cut and paste; the term existed in printing and publishing for centuries

lines.text: What actually happens when you copy and paste?
Hit copy, and your computer tucks it into a hidden spot called the clipboard,
lines.caps: HIT *COPY | AND YOUR *COMPUTER | *TUCKS IT | INTO A *HIDDEN SPOT | CALLED THE *CLIPBOARD

lines.text: which holds just one thing, so your next copy replaces it.
lines.caps: WHICH *HOLDS | JUST *ONE THING | SO YOUR *NEXT COPY | *REPLACES IT

lines.text: It saves your text in several formats at once,
and the app you paste into grabs the one it understands,
lines.caps: AND THE *APP | YOU *PASTE INTO | *GRABS THE ONE | IT *UNDERSTANDS

lines.text: which is why pasting into a plain notepad drops the bold.
lines.caps: WHICH IS *WHY | *PASTING INTO | A PLAIN *NOTEPAD | DROPS THE *BOLD

lines.text: And the name is older than computers.
Editors used to cut paragraphs out with scissors and paste them onto a new page.
lines.caps: *EDITORS | USED TO *CUT | *PARAGRAPHS OUT | WITH *SCISSORS | AND *PASTE THEM | ONTO A NEW *PAGE

lines.text: In the seventies, Larry Tesler at Xerox borrowed the words,
so every paste is really just digital scissors and glue.
